answer: Memory-hard identity audits make every seat prove it holds its own 2 GB working set. The set is a graph derived from the seat's key, and an audit names a random vertex whose label must be recomputed from its neighbours within 3 seconds, which only works if the whole graph sits in RAM. Audits hit all seats in the same instant, so an operator trying to forge 1,000 personas needs about 2 TB of resident memory, real copper and silicon bought per fake. Rebuilding the graph on demand or swapping to disk misses the deadline, and one graph can't serve two keys.
